messages.content: Four people, eight weeks, pull billing out of a monolith without freezing feature work. Give me the plan you would actually run.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=plan|construct=deeptree|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
Four people cannot staff a rewrite and a feature queue. A big-bang Friday cutover has no real rollback at this headcount. A shared database forever just moves the outage. The cut that fits is an HTTP strangle: new invoices go to a new service first, old reads stay, and the database split waits until the write path is quiet. Week 1 is the boundary plus a list of internal callers that don't go through HTTP, because a pure edge strangle misses those. The middle weeks shift traffic. The last two are leftover reads and a rollback drill.
</think>

Strangle it at the HTTP edge. New invoices go to a new service in week 1, old reads stay, and you don't split the database until writes are quiet. Week 1 also inventories internal callers that bypass HTTP. Last two weeks: leftover reads and one rollback drill.
I have one engineer and six weeks to move invoice email off the monolith without losing a receipt. The mail vendor stays. No feature freeze.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=plan|construct=deeptree|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
One person, so one boundary. Dual-write the receipt id for a week so a send exists in both logs before the cut. Then flip the sender. Then delete the old one only after a day of ids shows up only in the new log. Skipping the overlap is how a receipt disappears. Rewriting the monolith's mail stack is a second project.
</think>

Dual-write the receipt id for a week, cut the send over, then delete the old sender. The gate is a day of ids in both logs before the cut, and only in the new log after.
We need an on-call rotation for five people. Someone is out for two weeks in the middle. Don't give me a philosophy of burnout.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=plan|construct=deeptree|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
Five people, one slot at a time, and a two-week hole. The plan is a written rota with a named secondary, the gap filled by the two people on either side splitting those weeks, and no one doing more than one week in a row. Publishing it beats a Slack scramble. A shadow rotation of everyone watching everyone is not a plan.
</think>

Publish a weekly rota with a named secondary. Split the two-week absence between the people on either side of it. Nobody is primary two weeks running.
Move a reading group to a hall that is already booked for Wednesday. I need the sequence, not a vibe.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=plan|construct=deeptree|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
The hall is already booked, so 'book the hall' is not a step. The real sequence is confirm the hold, check whether the deposit is refundable until noon the day before, name who picks up the key that morning, and only then tell the group which room is the backup if the lights fail. Telling the group first creates a promise the key person hasn't accepted.
</think>

Confirm Wednesday's hold, check the deposit refunds until noon the day before, name the person who picks up the key, then tell the group the backup room.
A class of 20, one afternoon, teach them git rebase without a slide deck. Plan the hour.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=plan|construct=deeptree|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
They need one repo, one bad commit, and to see the commit id change. First 10 minutes: everyone clones the same tiny repo. Next 20: make a commit on main in the upstream that they don't have, then rebase and look at the new hash. Next 20: the case where they already pushed, and why rebase is now the wrong tool. Last 10: they say back what the hash changing means. A history lecture first will eat the hour.
</think>

Clone one tiny repo, make an upstream commit they don't have, rebase, and look at the new hash. Then show the already-pushed case, where rebase is the wrong tool. They restate what the new hash means before they leave.
Kitchen renovation, we still have to cook every night. Two weeks, one person who can be home at 3pm for deliveries. Plan it.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=plan|construct=deeptree|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
The constraint is dinner still happens. So the sink and one burner stay usable until the new ones are in, which means the work is sequenced as demo of the unused run first, deliveries at 3pm only, and a camp stove named as the fallback for the one night the sink is actually out. Doing the sink on day 1 strands dinner. Ordering everything for Monday when the person can only receive at 3pm wastes the morning slot.
</think>

Keep one burner and the sink until the replacements are in the room. Deliveries at 3pm only. The sink comes out on a night you already planned to use a camp stove, not on day one.
